newsitem.title: USA: Dole's all-out effort in California fails.
newsitem.headline: Dole's all-out effort in California fails.

text.p: Bob Dole's all-out effort to capture California's rich prize of electoral votes failed on Tuesday as President Bill Clinton comfortably captured the most populous state.
Clinton was winning the state and its haul of 54 electoral votes -- more than any other state -- with about 51 percent of the vote versus 39 percent for Republican challenger Dole.
But it was still too early to say by early Wednesday whether Clinton's coattails were long enough to help Democrats capture many California congressional seats.

California's congressional delegation was evenly divided 26-26 between Republicans and Democrats before the election and a large swing could have gone a long way towards giving the Democrats control of the House of Representatives.

Californians, fulfilling their reputation of setting new trends, voted for two controversial ballot initiatives. One measure will abolish most state affirmative action programmes that grant preferential treatment to racial minorities and women. Another makes it legal for sick people to smoke marijuana to ease their pain.
Democrat Walter Capps scored an upset in a Santa Barbara congressional race, appearing headed for a comfortable victory over freshman Republican incumbent Andrea Seastrand.
But the battle for several other key congressional seats was on a knife edge.
Long-time Republican congressman Bob Dornan of Garden Grove was in a neck-and-neck struggle with Democratic challenger Loretta Sanchez with about a third of the vote counted.

And with more than half of the vote counted, wealthy investment banker Ellen Tauscher, a Democrat, edged ahead of Republican incumbent Bill Baker by a fraction of a percentage point in another seat targeted by the Democrats.
Republican incumbent Frank Riggs won his close-fought race against 28-year-old Democrat Michela Alioto in his northern California district.

Speaking soon after Alioto called him to concede, Riggs told San Francisco's KPIX television: "We of course were worried because we recognised it was going to be a referendum on the Republican Congress. We just worked doubly hard, kept pressing ahead."

Clinton captured California in 1992 and assiduously courted Californians throughout his term, visiting the state 29 times and being quick to respond with federal aid when wildfires and earthquakes hit the state.

But in the final weeks of his campaign, Dole threw a lot of time and resources into an all-out effort to win California. A win would have given him one-fifth of the electoral votes needed for victory.
But political analysts said it was a risky strategy since it took money and resources away from other battleground states, effectively conceding them to Clinton.
Some analysts suggested that the strategy may have been aimed at boosting Republican voter turnout in California and re-electing Republican members of Congress.
